meta.titre: Economic Systems: how societies decide what, how and for whom to produce
meta.sous_theme: Traditional, market, planned and mixed economies; public goods

sections.contenu_markdown: In a village market in the Grassfields, traders and buyers agree on prices by bargaining. In another part of the country, the government builds a road, lights a street and pays for a school, and nobody pays a price at the gate. Every society has limited resources and unlimited wants, so it must decide what to produce, how to produce it and who receives it. The way a country answers these questions is its economic system. The GCE papers ask you to name systems from their features, to explain their advantages and disadvantages and to describe public goods.

items: Resources are scarce, while human wants are unlimited, so people must make choices.
Demand is the quantity that buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, and supply is the quantity that sellers offer at each price.
Goods and services can be provided by private firms or by the government.
Taxes are the main way in which a government gets money to provide services.

sections.titre: The four economic systems and the price mechanism
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The basic problem

Scarcity forces every society to answer three questions: **what** to produce, **how** to produce it and **for whom** to produce it. An **economic system** is the way a society organises production and distribution to answer them.

### The four systems

| System | Who decides | Main features |
|---|---|---|
| Traditional | Custom and tradition | Mostly subsistence farming, hunting and fishing, barter, little change over time |
| Market (free enterprise) | Buyers and sellers through prices | Private ownership, profit motive, competition, small role for government |
| Planned (command) | The government | State ownership of main resources, central plan, little private business |
| Mixed | Both market and government | Private and public sectors exist together |

### How a market economy works

The **price mechanism** is the way prices, set by the forces of demand and supply, guide the use of resources. A rising price signals that a good is scarce, so producers supply more and buyers buy less. A falling price signals the opposite. Producers follow profit, and consumers decide through their spending what is produced, which is called consumer sovereignty.

### Public goods

A **public good** is a good that:

- is **non-excludable**: nobody can easily be stopped from using it;
- is **non-rivalrous**: one person's use does not reduce what is left for others;
- is usually provided by the government and paid for out of taxes.

Street lighting and national defence are examples. Because people can use them without paying, private firms cannot make a profit, and this is the **free rider** problem.

variantes.nom: Advantages and disadvantages of a market economy
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to state and explain advantages of the market system
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Advantages**: resources are allocated by prices without a central authority; competition encourages efficiency and lower prices; the profit motive rewards effort and new ideas; consumers have a wide choice; and decisions are quick.

**Disadvantages**: wealth can be very unequal; firms do not supply public goods; monopolies can exploit consumers; and goods that harm others, such as pollution, may be ignored.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about government control of production
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Advantages**: resources can be directed to national needs, public goods and basic services are provided, and income can be shared more equally.

**Disadvantages**: a central authority cannot know every want, so there may be shortages or unsold goods; workers and managers have little incentive to work hard or to innovate; consumers have little choice; and the system needs a large bureaucracy.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks why most countries combine the systems
variantes.contenu_markdown: In a mixed economy private firms produce most consumer goods, while the government provides public goods, runs some enterprises and regulates the market. Most countries today are mixed, because each pure system has weaknesses that the other can correct.

sections.enonce_markdown: State and explain THREE disadvantages of a planned economy. (6 marks)

etapes.justification: "State and explain" requires a point and a reason for each, so a list alone earns half the marks.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Three disadvantages, each with an explanation, each worth 2 marks.

etapes.action: Recall the definition and choose three relevant points.
etapes.justification: A planned economy is directed by a central authority, and the disadvantages come from that centralisation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Points chosen: shortages and surpluses, lack of incentives, limited consumer choice.

etapes.justification: Planners cannot know the wants of millions of people without price signals.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Some goods are produced in too large a quantity and remain unsold, while others are scarce.

etapes.justification: The state owns the resources and workers do not earn profit.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Workers and managers have little reason to work harder or to innovate; and consumers must accept what the plan produces, with little choice.

etapes.justification: A conclusion links the points to the question without adding new ideas.
etapes.resultat_markdown: These weaknesses explain why most countries allow private business next to the state.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** (1) Shortages and surpluses: planners must guess the wants of the people without price signals, so some goods are produced in excess and others are scarce. (2) Lack of incentives: workers and managers do not keep any profit from extra effort, so they have little reason to work harder or to find better methods. (3) Limited choice: the plan decides what is produced, so consumers must accept the goods available instead of choosing what they prefer. Award 1 mark for each point stated and 1 mark for each explanation.

items.erreur_markdown: "In a market economy the government makes all the decisions about prices."
items.pourquoi_faux: In a market economy prices come from the interaction of demand and supply. A government that sets all prices belongs to a planned system.
items.correction_markdown: In a market economy prices are determined by demand and supply and guide the use of resources.

items.erreur_markdown: "A public good is any good provided by the government, such as a government car."
items.pourquoi_faux: A public good is defined by its features: it is non-excludable and non-rivalrous. A car bought by the state can only be used by one person at a time, so it is not a public good.
items.correction_markdown: A public good is non-excludable and non-rivalrous, for example street lighting.

items.erreur_markdown: "A traditional economy is a planned economy, because customs plan what people do."
items.pourquoi_faux: In a traditional economy decisions follow custom, not a plan made by a central authority.
items.correction_markdown: A traditional economy is guided by custom and tradition; a planned economy is guided by a government plan.

items.erreur_markdown: Question: State and explain three advantages of a market economy. Answer: "Competition, choice, profit."
items.pourquoi_faux: The answer states three words but explains none, so it earns only about half of the marks.
items.correction_markdown: Write a sentence for each point, for example: competition forces firms to use resources efficiently and to keep prices low.

items.enonce_markdown:
Name the economic system described in each statement.

(a) Decisions follow customs handed down from earlier generations.

(b) A central authority decides what, how and for whom to produce.

(c) Prices set by demand and supply allocate resources and private firms seek profit.

(d) Private firms and the government both play an important part.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Traditional economy**. (b) **Planned (command) economy**. (c) **Market (free enterprise) economy**. (d) **Mixed economy**.

Award one mark for each correct system.

items.enonce_markdown:
The table shows the weekly demand and supply of tomatoes in a market.

| Price per kg (FCFA) | Quantity demanded (kg) | Quantity supplied (kg) |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 90 | 10 |
| 200 | 70 | 30 |
| 300 | 50 | 50 |
| 400 | 30 | 70 |
| 500 | 10 | 90 |

(a) State the equilibrium price and quantity.

(b) What happens at a price of 200 FCFA, and how does the price mechanism correct it?

(c) What happens at a price of 400 FCFA?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: price **300 FCFA** and quantity **50 kg**.

(b) At 200 FCFA demand is 70 kg and supply is 30 kg, so there is a **shortage of 40 kg**. Buyers compete for the tomatoes and sellers raise the price. A higher price increases the quantity supplied and reduces the quantity demanded until the shortage disappears at 300 FCFA.

(c) At 400 FCFA supply is 70 kg and demand is 30 kg, so there is a **surplus of 40 kg**. Sellers lower the price to sell the stock, which reduces the quantity supplied and increases the quantity demanded until the price returns to 300 FCFA.

items.enonce_markdown: Discuss why most countries have a mixed economy instead of a pure market economy or a pure planned economy. (6 marks)
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for the following points (maximum 6).

- A pure market economy leaves out public goods such as street lighting and defence, which firms cannot sell for a profit, so the government must provide them (1 mark for the point, 1 for the reason).
- A pure market economy can produce large inequalities and monopolies, so the government regulates, taxes and helps the poor (2 marks).
- A pure planned economy gives little incentive, little choice and many errors of planning, so private business and prices are used to improve efficiency (2 marks).
- Conclusion: a mixed economy combines the efficiency and choice of markets with the fairness and public services provided by the government (1 mark).

Key idea: **each pure system has weaknesses that the other system corrects**.

items_markdown: Scarcity forces every society to decide what, how and for whom to produce; the economic system is the way it does so.
Traditional economies follow custom, market economies follow prices, planned economies follow a government plan and mixed economies combine market and government.
In a market economy prices set by demand and supply allocate resources, firms seek profit and consumers are sovereign.
Advantages of the market system are efficiency, choice and incentives; its disadvantages are inequality, monopoly and the neglect of public goods.
A public good is non-excludable and non-rivalrous, is usually paid for out of taxes and creates the free rider problem.
